title: Designing the Day (PGAV Destinations)
why_it_matters: A working master planner explains attractions-per-hour-per-guest, peak-hour time budgets and how attraction mix is sized.

title: Theme Park Master Planning (Peter Alexander, ThemedAttraction.com)
why_it_matters: Plain-language walk through feasibility, design day, entertainment units, layout choices and attraction mix from a veteran planner.

title: How to Design a Theme Park: Master Planning Process (Falcon's Creative Group)
why_it_matters: Describes the layered master-planning method: questions first, site analysis, loose alternatives, content planning and constraints.

title: Jeff Havlik, PGAV Destinations (Blooloop profile)
why_it_matters: Profile of a master planner whose operational programme ties every part of a park to attendance targets.

title: Managing Extremes: Seasonality & Peaking of a Theme Park (The Park Database)
why_it_matters: Uses Tokyo Disney Resort data to show how design day is derived from peak month, peak week and peak day.

title: Disney utilidor system (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Overview of the Magic Kingdom service tunnels: size, dates, why they sit at ground level, and the smaller Epcot system.

title: The Utilidors: inside the Magic Kingdom's secret underground city (ClickOrlando)
why_it_matters: Reported figures on the tunnels: 9 acres, 29 access points, AVAC trash system, raised site, Dick Nunis on Walt's intent.

title: The secret tunnels of Disney's Magic Kingdom theme park (Amusement Logic)
why_it_matters: A design firm's short explainer on how swampy ground pushed the tunnels to grade and the park one storey up.

title: Harrison Price, Disney Legend (D23)
why_it_matters: Official biography of the economist who ran the 1953 Disneyland site study and founded Economics Research Associates.

title: Walt's Revolution! By the Numbers (Harrison Price, 2004)
why_it_matters: Price's own account of feasibility studies, site selection and attendance forecasting for Disney and other parks.

title: Disneyland (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Reference for the 1955 opening, the 160-acre Anaheim site, the Stanford Research Institute study, the hub and the berm.

title: Magic Kingdom (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Reference for the 1971 opening, hub-and-spoke plan, Seven Seas Lagoon fill, raised park and top-ranked attendance.

title: Walt Disney World (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Scale of a destination resort: roughly 27,000 acres, four parks, two water parks and dozens of hotels bought as the Florida Project.

title: Transportation and Ticket Center (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: The classic park-and-transfer model: 12,156-space lot, trams, then monorail or ferry across the lagoon to the gate.

title: Reedy Creek Improvement District (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: How a resort runs its own utilities, building codes and fire service: power, chilled water, wastewater and the EPCOT Building Codes.

title: Life Safety Code, NFPA 101 (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Summary of the US code that governs means of egress and assembly occupancies, which shapes park evacuation routes.

title: Capacity Analysis of Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities (FHWA-HRT-98-107)
why_it_matters: Tabulates walkway level-of-service thresholds in square metres per pedestrian, comparing Fruin's values with the Highway Capacity Manual.

title: Pedestrian Planning and Design (John J. Fruin, 1971)
why_it_matters: The original source of pedestrian level of service, body ellipse and walkway capacity used by crowd planners.

title: Crowd Dynamics, PhD thesis chapter 3 (G. Keith Still)
why_it_matters: Critical review of Fruin level of service, the 4 persons per square metre guidance and flow rates for moving crowds.

title: Crowd density: static and dynamic spaces (G. Keith Still)
why_it_matters: Explains why standing crowds and moving crowds need different density limits, with visual density references.

title: An Urban Designer Looks at Main Street (Sam Gennawey, TouringPlans)
why_it_matters: An urban planner reads the arrival sequence, hub and castle weenie of Magic Kingdom as city design.

title: The Image of the City (Kevin Lynch, 1960)
why_it_matters: Paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks: the mental-map vocabulary park planners borrow for legibility.

title: The Social Logic of Space (Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson, 1984)
why_it_matters: The founding text of space syntax, which predicts movement from the shape of a street or path network.

title: Space syntax (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Accessible overview of axial lines, isovists, integration and choice measures and their origin at UCL.

title: Space Syntax Online Training Platform (UCL and Space Syntax Ltd)
why_it_matters: Free training site with tutorials and software guides for running space syntax analysis on a layout.

title: Designing Disney: Imagineering and the Art of the Show (John Hench, 2003)
why_it_matters: A founding Imagineer on how park layout, transitions and the hub were designed to feel welcoming.

title: Bill Evans, Disney Legend (D23)
why_it_matters: Biography of the landscape architect who turned Anaheim orange groves into Disneyland's planted worlds in about a year.

title: Official Release of the 2024 TEA Global Experience Index
why_it_matters: The annual attendance report: top 25 theme parks reached almost 246 million visits in 2024, up 2.4 percent.

title: What is the Theme Index & Museum Index? (TEA)
why_it_matters: Landing page describing the free global attendance study and linking past editions.

title: Theme Index and Museum Index (AECOM)
why_it_matters: AECOM's archive page for the TEA/AECOM Theme Index editions used to benchmark park attendance.

title: Universal Epic Universe (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: A 2025 hub-and-spoke park: Celestial Park hub, four portal worlds, about 110 acres inside a 750-acre site.

title: Universal Epic Universe: everything we know (Discover Universal blog)
why_it_matters: Universal's own description of the entry through Chronos, Celestial Park and the four portals.

title: Epic Universe map and layout analysis (Mappedin)
why_it_matters: Reads the park plan as immersion traded against legibility: sealed worlds, hidden portals, one hub.

title: Universal Islands of Adventure (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Example of a loop layout: Port of Entry then islands arranged around a central lagoon, opened 1999.

title: Universal Studios Florida (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: A 1990 park whose themed areas sit around a central lagoon, the classic loop plan.

title: Tokyo DisneySea (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Ports of call around a harbour with Mount Prometheus as icon; Fantasy Springs expansion opened in 2024.

title: Europa-Park (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: A family-owned park that grew from 16 hectares in 1975 into a resort with country-themed areas and six hotels.

title: Ferrari World Abu Dhabi (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: A mostly indoor park opened in 2010 on Yas Island, built for a hot climate under one large roof.

title: Warner Bros. World Abu Dhabi (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Fully indoor, air-conditioned park opened 2018 with six themed areas designed by Thinkwell.

title: Water park (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: Definition, typical attractions, market size and the trade bodies for water parks.

title: World Waterpark Association
why_it_matters: The industry association for water parks: trade show, magazine, safety campaigns and supplier directory.

title: Disney's Typhoon Lagoon (Wikipedia)
why_it_matters: A water park planned around a central wave pool and mountain with a lazy river loop around the whole site.
